input:
Emissions sampling has one central requirement that is easy to state but easy to get wrong in practice: the sample that is analysed must represent the emission as a whole, because every conclusion drawn from the analysis will be applied to the whole gas stream and not merely to the portion that happened to enter the sampling line. Where samples are taken is the first decision. The sampling position should be at a location where the gas is well mixed, since a sample drawn from a poorly mixed region may reflect a local pocket of gas rather than the stream average, and positions close to disturbances that disturb the flow, or where deposits accumulate, carry the same risk. The second point concerns how a sample is built up. A single sample is formed from a number of increments, which are small portions collected at intervals over the sampling period and combined before analysis, so that the sample reflects conditions across the period rather than at one instant of it. This matters because a single grab sample, taken at one moment and analysed on its own, can mislead in either direction: the emission varies as operating conditions vary, concentrations are not uniform across the duct, and a moment that is convenient for sampling may be quite untypical of the emission over the period the result is meant to describe. A sample built from increments taken at a representative position does not remove all uncertainty, but it matches the quantity being reported, which is the emission over a period, rather than the state of the gas at a single point in space and time.

The increments also need to be spread across the operating cycle of the source, because an emission that follows a process cycle will present different concentrations at different stages of that cycle, and increments clustered in a quiet stage would understate the emission just as surely as increments clustered in a peak stage would overstate it, even if every individual increment were collected and analysed correctly.
target:
A sample of a gas emission must represent the emission as a whole. Every conclusion from the analysis is applied to the whole gas stream, not to the portion that entered the sampling line. Sampling position is the first decision. Samples are taken where the gas is well mixed. A sample drawn from a poorly mixed region reflects a local pocket of gas, not the stream average, and positions close to flow disturbances, or where deposits accumulate, carry the same risk. Sample construction is the second decision. One sample is formed from a number of increments: small portions collected at intervals over the sampling period and combined before analysis. A combined sample reflects conditions across the period. A single grab sample misleads. Emission strength varies as operating conditions vary, concentration is not uniform across the duct, and a moment convenient for sampling can be untypical of the emission over the period the result describes. A grab sample can therefore sit above or below the period average, with nothing in the sample itself to show the direction of the error. Increments taken at a representative position match the sample to the quantity reported: the emission over a period, not the state of the gas at a single point in space and time.

Increment timing carries the same requirement. Increments are spread across the operating cycle of the source. An emission that follows a process cycle presents different concentrations at different stages of the cycle. Increments clustered in a quiet stage understate the emission. Increments clustered in a peak stage overstate the emission. Correct collection and analysis of each increment do not repair a biased spread. The sampling line also draws from the main body of the gas. A stagnant pocket near a wall or a dead leg gives increments from gas that is not moving with the stream, and increments of that kind misrepresent the emission however carefully the later stages are handled. Position, increment spread and sample construction act together: a defect in any one of them passes into the reported result.
